report:
### Conclusion
The health claim is **true**: strong scientific evidence demonstrates that add-on pharmaceutical cannabidiol (CBD) significantly reduces convulsive seizure frequency in children with drug-resistant Dravet syndrome.

### Evidence Summary

* **Landmark Trial Results:** A Phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in *The New England Journal of Medicine* showed that adjunctive oral CBD reduced median monthly convulsive seizures from 12.4 to 5.9 (a 39% reduction), compared to a minor change from 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo ([NEJM Trial](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618?__cf_chl_jschl_tk__=eoIiI4VLubYou1rYBhIMWYDermXOBMChKpsJg_zIU9Q-1639612923-0-gaNycGzNCdE)).
* **Dose-Ranging Efficacy:** Clinical studies evaluating daily adjunctive CBD doses of 10 mg/kg and 20 mg/kg demonstrated convulsive seizure reductions of 48.7% and 45.7% from baseline, respectively ([PMC Systematic Review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10949818/)).
* **Regulatory Approvals:** Based on these clinical trials, regulatory authorities including the U.S. FDA approved Epidiolex (a purified oral CBD solution) as an effective adjunctive treatment for Dravet syndrome ([FDA Drug Label](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2018/210365lbl.pdf); [US Pharmacist Review](https://www.uspharmacist.com/article/cannabidiol)).

While adjunctive CBD carries potential adverse effects (such as somnolence and elevated liver enzymes) that require clinical monitoring, randomized trials consistently confirm its efficacy in lowering convulsive seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome.
